youtube.title: Robert Smalls Sailed Past Fort Sumter
youtube.description:
Congress paid him $5,000 for the ship he commandeered.
On May 13, 1862, enslaved Robert Smalls commandeered the Confederate ship Planter with seven crewmen aboard. Wearing the captain's straw hat and copying his manners, he sailed past Fort Sumter at 4:30 a.m. giving the correct signals. The Planter became a Union warship, freeing Smalls and his crew's families.
Sources: Wikipedia - Robert Smalls, Wikipedia - USS Robert Smalls
#Shorts #RobertSmalls #History #TrueStory

notes: Robert Smalls (April 5, 1839 – February 23, 1915) was an American politician who was born into slavery in Beaufort, South Carolina.
During the American Civil War, the still enslaved Smalls commandeered a Confederate transport ship in Charleston Harbor and sailed it from the Confederate-controlled waters of the harbor to the U.S.
blockade that surrounded it.
He then piloted the ship to the Union-controlled enclave in the Beaufort–Port Royal–Hilton Head area, where it became a Union warship.
In the process, he freed himself, his crew, and their families.
His example and persuasion helped convince President Abraham Lincoln to accept black soldiers into the Union Army.
Robert Smalls was born on April 5, 1839, in Beaufort, South Carolina, to Lydia Polite, a woman enslaved by Henry McKee.
At age 17, Smalls married Hannah Jones, an enslaved hotel maid, in Charleston on December 24, 1856.
Smalls aimed to pay for their freedom by purchasing them outright, but the price was steep, $800 (equivalent to $28,667 in 2025).
In April 1861, the Civil War began with the Battle of Fort Sumter in nearby Charleston Harbor.
Smalls appeared content and had the confidence of the Planter's crew and owners, but, at some time in April 1862, he began to plan an escape.
On May 12, 1862, the Planter traveled ten miles southwest of Charleston to stop at Coles Island, a Confederate post on the Stono River that was being dismantled.
on May 13, Smalls and seven of the eight enslaved crewmen made their previously planned escape to the Union blockade ships.
Smalls guided the ship past the five Confederate harbor forts without incident, as he gave the correct steam-whistle signals at checkpoints.
Relyea, and Smalls copied Relyea's manners and straw hat on deck to fool Confederate onlookers from shore and the forts.
The Planter sailed past Fort Sumter at about 4:30 a.m.
When Fort Sumter flashed the challenge signal, Smalls again gave the correct hand signs.
Finally, the fort signaled that all was well, and Smalls sailed his ship out of the harbor.
Most valuable, however, were the captain's code book containing the Confederate signals and a map of the mines and torpedoes that had been laid in Charleston's harbor.
However, with the encouragement of Major General David Hunter, the Union commander at Port Royal, Smalls went to Washington, D.C., in August 1862 with Rev.

He was made pilot of the ironclad USS Keokuk, again under Captain Rhind, and took part in the attack on Fort Sumter on April 7, 1863, which was a preamble to the Second Battle of Fort Sumter later that fall.
On December 1, 1863, Smalls was piloting the Planter under Captain James Nickerson on Folly Island Creek when Confederate batteries at Secessionville opened fire.
Smalls returned with the Planter to Charleston harbor in April 1865 for the ceremonial raising of the American flag again at Fort Sumter.
Many sources also state that General Gillmore promoted Smalls to captain in December 1863 after he saved the Planter when it was under attack near Secessionville.

In 1883, during discussion of the bill to put Smalls on the Navy retired list, a report stated that the 1862 appraisal of the Planter was "absurdly low" and that a fair valuation would have been more than $60,000.
That year, Congress passed a statute paying Smalls $5,000, less the amount paid to him in 1862 ($1,500), for his capture of the steamship.

The monument to Smalls in this churchyard is inscribed with his 1895 statement to the South Carolina legislature: "My race needs no special defense, for the past history of them in this country proves them to be the equal of any people anywhere.
Fort Robert Smalls was named in his honor; it was built by free blacks in 1863 on McGuire's Hill on the South Side of Pittsburgh during the Civil War.
In 2004, the United States named a ship for Smalls, the USAV Major General Robert Smalls (LSV-8), a Kuroda-class logistics support vessel operated by the U.S.
In March 2023, she was renamed for Robert Smalls, a former slave who freed himself and others by commandeering a Confederate transport ship.

During the 2020 George Floyd protests, the name of the ship came into question because it honored a victory of the Confederate army fighting against the United States for southern independence and in defense of slavery.

On 27 February 2023, the Secretary of the Navy Carlos Del Toro announced that the US Navy would rename Chancellorsville after Robert Smalls, a slave who commandeered the Confederate ship CSS Planter in 1862.
